turns.content: Hi, I'm working on an article about child and maternal health in Colombia, Peru, and Chile. Could you help me get the latest key data and explain the main concepts clearly?

**Summary (for your article):**  
As of the early 2020s, Chile has the lowest child and maternal mortality among the three, while Colombia and Peru have made major gains but still face higher risks—especially around adolescent pregnancy and maternal deaths. All three have very high coverage of skilled birth attendance; Peru’s nutrition and contraceptive data highlight both progress and remaining gaps.

---

## Data

### 1. Child survival

**Under‑5 mortality rate, 2023 (per 1,000 live births)**

| Country   | Under‑5 mortality (2023) |
|----------|---------------------------|
| Chile    | <claim id="8ed10239" policy="auto">7.2</claim> |
| Colombia | <claim id="f78e1b01" policy="auto">12.0</claim> |
| Peru     | <claim id="30596b53" policy="auto">15.8</claim> |

**Neonatal mortality rate, 2023 (deaths in first 28 days per 1,000 live births)**

| Country   | Neonatal mortality (2023) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| Chile    | <claim id="5f1a8627" policy="auto">4.6</claim> |
| Colombia | <claim id="2c89c155" policy="auto">6.5</claim> |
| Peru     | <claim id="c426d4ba" policy="auto">7.8</claim> |

### 2. Maternal survival

**Maternal mortality ratio, 2023 (per 100,000 live births, modeled estimates)**

| Country   | MMR (2023) |
|----------|------------|
| Chile    | <claim id="a693f2f4" policy="auto">10</claim> |
| Colombia | <claim id="9e397587" policy="auto">59</claim> |
| Peru     | <claim id="2e75d199" policy="auto">51</claim> |

### 3. Coverage of key services

**Births attended by skilled health staff (% of total births, latest WDI)**

| Country   | Year | Skilled birth attendance |
|----------|------|--------------------------|
| Chile    | 2019 | <claim id="efcc718e" policy="auto">99.8</claim>% |
| Colombia | 2019 | <claim id="de9bd242" policy="auto">98.8</claim>% |
| Peru     | 2021 | <claim id="c1ffa4be" policy="auto">94.9</claim>% |

**Antenatal care, at least one visit (% of pregnant women, latest available)**

| Country | Year | At least 1 ANC visit |
|---------|------|----------------------|
| Peru    | 2020 | <claim id="b8cb8c36" policy="auto">98.1</claim>% |

*(No recent WDI values for this specific indicator for Colombia and Chile.)*

### 4. Child nutrition (Peru as an example)

**Peru – child undernutrition (latest WDI)**

| Indicator                                              | Year | Value |
|--------------------------------------------------------|------|-------|
| Stunting, height‑for‑age (% of children under 5)       | 2023 | <claim id="8464ea8a" policy="auto">11.5</claim>% |
| Wasting, weight‑for‑height (% of children under 5)     | 2023 | <claim id="5a7bb741" policy="auto">0.6</claim>%  |

### 5. Adolescent fertility & contraception

**Adolescent fertility rate, 2023 (births per 1,000 women aged 15–19)**

| Country   | Adolescent fertility (2023) |
|----------|------------------------------|
| Chile    | <claim id="95148b00" policy="auto">6.542</claim> |
| Peru     | <claim id="fa7d452e" policy="auto">43.562</claim> |
| Colombia | <claim id="26232d7e" policy="auto">59.473</claim> |

**Contraceptive prevalence, modern methods (% of married women 15–49, Peru)**

| Country | Year | Modern contraceptive prevalence |
|---------|------|---------------------------------|
| Peru    | 2023 | <claim id="b33d8cb8" policy="auto">57.9</claim>% |

---

## Analysis (narrative you can adapt)

You could structure your article around three themes: **survival**, **services**, and **sexual and reproductive health**.

### A. Child survival: strong progress, but differences remain

- Across all three countries, child deaths are now relatively low by global standards. Under‑5 mortality ranges from about <claim id="8ed10239" policy="auto">7.2</claim> per 1,000 live births in Chile to <claim id="15.8" policy="auto">15.8</claim> in Peru (2023).  
- Neonatal deaths account for a large share of under‑5 deaths. Neonatal mortality is <claim id="5f1a8627" policy="auto">4.6</claim> in Chile, <claim id="2c89c155" policy="auto">6.5</claim> in Colombia, and <claim id="c426d4ba" policy="auto">7.8</claim> in Peru per 1,000 live births (2023).  
- For your narrative: you can emphasize that **most children now survive to their fifth birthday**, but that **the first month of life is still the riskiest period**, especially in Peru and Colombia.

### B. Maternal survival: Chile is near high‑income levels; Peru and Colombia still higher risk

- Chile’s maternal mortality ratio is very low at around <claim id="a693f2f4" policy="auto">10</claim> deaths per 100,000 live births (2023), comparable to many high‑income countries.  
- Colombia and Peru have higher ratios—<claim id="9e397587" policy="auto">59</claim> and <claim id="2e75d199" policy="auto">51</claim> respectively (2023). That means a woman giving birth in Colombia or Peru still faces roughly **five to six times** the risk of dying from pregnancy‑related causes compared with a woman in Chile.  
- These modeled estimates reflect not only health care quality but also broader social determinants—poverty, geography, and inequities affecting Indigenous and rural women.

### C. Service coverage: near‑universal skilled attendance, but gaps in quality and continuity

- Skilled birth attendance is almost universal in all three countries: above <claim id="efcc718e" policy="auto">99.8</claim>% in Chile, <claim id="de9bd242" policy="auto">98.8</claim>% in Colombia, and <claim id="c1ffa4be" policy="auto">94.9</claim>% in Peru (latest years).  
- In Peru, at least one antenatal care visit covers about <claim id="b8cb8c36" policy="auto">98.1</claim>% of pregnant women (2020).  
- For your article, you can stress that **the challenge is less about contact with the health system and more about the quality and timeliness of care**—for example, whether complications are recognized early and whether emergency obstetric services are available everywhere.

### D. Child nutrition: chronic undernutrition persists in Peru

- In Peru, about <claim id="8464ea8a" policy="auto">11.5</claim>% of children under 5 are stunted (too short for their age) as of 2023, while wasting affects only <claim id="5a7bb741" policy="auto">0.6</claim>%.  
- This pattern—**moderate stunting but very low wasting**—is typical of countries where chronic deprivation (diet, sanitation, early‑life infections) is more important than acute food crises.  
- For Colombia and Chile, you may need to complement this with national survey reports, but regionally both have lower stunting than Peru, with remaining pockets among poorer and Indigenous communities.

### E. Adolescent fertility and contraception: big contrasts

- Adolescent fertility is very low in Chile—about <claim id="95148b00" policy="auto">6.542</claim> births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19 in 2023—similar to Western Europe.  
- In contrast, Colombia and Peru have much higher adolescent fertility: about <claim id="26232d7e" policy="auto">59.473</claim> in Colombia and <claim id="fa7d452e" policy="auto">43.562</claim> in Peru per 1,000 girls 15–19.  
- In Peru, modern contraceptive use among married women 15–49 is around <claim id="b33d8cb8" policy="auto">57.9</claim>% (2023). That suggests large room to expand access and choice, especially for adolescents and unmarried women (who are not covered by this particular indicator).  
- For your article: you can argue that **early and unintended pregnancy remains a major frontier issue** in Colombia and Peru, with clear implications for girls’ education, income, and intergenerational poverty.

---

## Concepts – short, article‑friendly definitions

You can drop these as sidebars or glossaries:

- **Under‑5 mortality rate** – Number of children who die before their fifth birthday per 1,000 live births. A summary of how safe it is to be a child in a country.  
- **Neonatal mortality rate** – Number of babies who die in the first 28 days after birth per 1,000 live births. Highly sensitive to the quality of care around childbirth and maternal health.  
- **Maternal mortality ratio** – Number of women who die from pregnancy‑related causes per 100,000 live births. A core measure of how safe pregnancy and childbirth are.  
- **Skilled birth attendance** – Percentage of births assisted by trained health professionals (doctors, nurses, midwives) who can manage complications.  
- **Antenatal (prenatal) care coverage** – Percentage of pregnant women who see a trained provider during pregnancy. At least one visit is a minimum; multiple visits are better.  
- **Stunting** – When a child is too short for their age because of long‑term poor nutrition and infections. It affects brain development, school performance, and adult earnings.  
- **Wasting** – When a child is too thin for their height, usually due to recent illness or food shortage. It is closely linked to risk of death.  
- **Adolescent fertility rate** – Number of births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19. High rates reflect gaps in sexual education, contraception, and gender equality.  
- **Contraceptive prevalence (modern methods)** – Share of women of reproductive age using modern contraceptives (e.g., pills, IUDs, implants, condoms). Indicates how well women can control if and when to have children.

---

## Sources:

- **World Bank — World Development Indicators (WB_WDI)**  
  - Mortality rate, under‑5 (per 1,000 live births)  
  - Mortality rate, neonatal (per 1,000 live births)  
  - Maternal mortality ratio (modeled estimate, per 100,000 live births)  
  - Births attended by skilled health staff (% of total)  
  - Pregnant women receiving prenatal care (%)  
  - Prevalence of stunting and wasting (% of children under 5)  
  - Adolescent fertility rate (births per 1,000 women ages 15–19)  
  - Contraceptive prevalence, any modern method (% of married women ages 15–49)

---

**Suggested follow-ups:**

1. Could you show how these indicators have changed since 2000 for each country, to highlight progress and setbacks over time?  
2. Can we break down any of these indicators by income group or region within each country (e.g., rural vs urban, poorest vs richest)?  
3. Can you help me draft 2–3 short country profiles (one per country) that weave these numbers into a narrative for a general audience?

**Intent:** You’re writing an article on child and maternal health in Colombia, Peru, and Chile, and you want the latest key data plus clear explanations of the main concepts.

**Selection Logic:**  
I focused on widely used World Bank / UN-style indicators that capture core aspects of maternal and child health and have recent data for all three countries:

- Child survival: under‑5 mortality, neonatal mortality  
- Maternal survival: maternal mortality ratio  
- Service coverage: skilled birth attendance, antenatal care  
- Child nutrition: stunting and wasting (note: only Peru has recent data here in WDI)  
- Reproductive health: adolescent fertility, contraceptive prevalence  

All data below come from the World Development Indicators (WB_WDI), which are standard for cross‑country comparison.

**Data Gaps (from tool calls):**

- Skilled birth attendance (% of births attended by skilled staff):  
  - Latest data: Chile <claim id="efcc718e" policy="auto">99.8</claim>% (2019), Colombia <claim id="de9bd242" policy="auto">98.8</claim>% (2019), Peru <claim id="c1ffa4be" policy="auto">94.9</claim>% (2021). No newer values yet in WDI.
- Antenatal care coverage (pregnant women receiving prenatal care, at least one visit):  
  - Only Peru has recent WDI data: <claim id="b8cb8c36" policy="auto">98.1</claim>% (2020). No recent WDI data for Colombia and Chile for this specific indicator.
- Nutrition (stunting & wasting):  
  - Stunting (height‑for‑age, % under 5): recent WDI data available only for Peru: <claim id="8464ea8a" policy="auto">11.5</claim>% (2023).  
  - Wasting (weight‑for‑height, % under 5): again only Peru: <claim id="5a7bb741" policy="auto">0.6</claim>% (2023).  
  - For Colombia and Chile, WDI doesn’t list very recent values for these exact codes; national surveys may have newer figures but are outside this tool set.
- Contraceptive prevalence (modern methods, married women 15–49):  
  - Recent data only for Peru in WDI: <claim id="b33d8cb8" policy="auto">57.9</claim>% (2023). No comparable recent WDI series for Colombia and Chile under this exact definition.

**Key Latest Data (using latest available year in WDI):**

_All mortality rates are per 1,000 live births unless noted; maternal mortality is per 100,000 live births; adolescent fertility is births per 1,000 women 15–19._

1. **Under‑5 mortality (2023)**  
   - Chile: <claim id="8ed10239" policy="auto">7.2</claim>  
   - Colombia: <claim id="f78e1b01" policy="auto">12.0</claim>  
   - Peru: <claim id="30596b53" policy="auto">15.8</claim>  

2. **Neonatal mortality (deaths in first 28 days, 2023)**  
   - Chile: <claim id="5f1a8627" policy="auto">4.6</claim>  
   - Colombia: <claim id="2c89c155" policy="auto">6.5</claim>  
   - Peru: <claim id="c426d4ba" policy="auto">7.8</claim>  

3. **Maternal mortality ratio (modeled, per 100,000 live births, 2023)**  
   - Chile: <claim id="a693f2f4" policy="auto">10</claim>  
   - Colombia: <claim id="9e397587" policy="auto">59</claim>  
   - Peru: <claim id="2e75d199" policy="auto">51</claim>  

4. **Skilled birth attendance (% of births, latest)**  
   - Chile: <claim id="efcc718e" policy="auto">99.8</claim>% (2019)  
   - Colombia: <claim id="de9bd242" policy="auto">98.8</claim>% (2019)  
   - Peru: <claim id="c1ffa4be" policy="auto">94.9</claim>% (2021)  

5. **Antenatal care, at least one visit (% of pregnant women, latest)**  
   - Peru: <claim id="b8cb8c36" policy="auto">98.1</claim>% (2020)  

6. **Child nutrition (Peru only, latest WDI)**  
   - Stunting, under‑5: <claim id="8464ea8a" policy="auto">11.5</claim>% (2023)  
   - Wasting, under‑5: <claim id="5a7bb741" policy="auto">0.6</claim>% (2023)  

7. **Adolescent fertility rate (births per 1,000 women 15–19, 2023)**  
   - Chile: <claim id="95148b00" policy="auto">6.542</claim>  
   - Peru: <claim id="fa7d452e" policy="auto">43.562</claim>  
   - Colombia: <claim id="26232d7e" policy="auto">59.473</claim>  

8. **Contraceptive prevalence, modern methods (% of married women 15–49, Peru)**  
   - Peru: <claim id="b33d8cb8" policy="auto">57.9</claim>% (2023)  

**Concept Explanations (for your article):**

You can frame these as short “What does this mean?” boxes:

- **Under‑5 mortality rate**: probability that a newborn will die before reaching age 5, per 1,000 live births. It summarizes overall conditions for young children: infections, nutrition, injuries, and the strength of primary health care.  

- **Neonatal mortality rate**: deaths in the first 28 days of life per 1,000 live births. This is strongly linked to maternal health, quality of care around birth, and complications like prematurity, birth asphyxia, and infections.  

- **Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)**: number of women who die from pregnancy‑related causes while pregnant or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy, per 100,000 live births. It reflects the safety of pregnancy and childbirth, access to emergency obstetric care, and broader inequalities.  

- **Births attended by skilled health staff**: share of deliveries attended by trained health professionals (doctors, nurses, midwives). High coverage is essential to manage complications and reduce both maternal and newborn deaths.  

- **Antenatal (prenatal) care coverage**: share of pregnant women who receive care during pregnancy from skilled providers. At least one visit is the minimum; many guidelines now emphasize 8+ contacts. It’s used to detect risks early (e.g., high blood pressure, anemia, infections).  

- **Stunting (low height‑for‑age)**: chronic undernutrition in early life, measured as children under 5 whose height is too low for their age. It reflects long‑term deprivation (poor diet, infections) and is linked to worse school performance and adult earnings.  

- **Wasting (low weight‑for‑height)**: acute undernutrition, often due to recent illness or food shortage. Children with wasting are at higher risk of death in the short term.  

- **Adolescent fertility rate**: number of births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19. High rates often signal gaps in sexual education, contraception access, and gender equality, and are associated with higher health risks for both young mothers and their babies.  

- **Contraceptive prevalence (modern methods)**: share of women of reproductive age (here, married 15–49) using modern contraceptive methods. Higher use is usually associated with lower unintended pregnancy, lower adolescent fertility, and better spacing of births.

**CLARIFYING QUESTION:**  
Do you want to go deeper into **trends over the last 10–20 years** and **inequalities (e.g., rural vs urban, poorest vs richest)** for these three countries, or is your article mainly focused on a **snapshot comparison of current levels**?

turns.content: Could you please provide the trends for these key indicators since 2000 to show how child and maternal health outcomes have evolved in each country?

**Summary:** Since 2000, all three countries have sharply reduced child and maternal deaths. Chile started from lower levels and now approaches high‑income benchmarks; Colombia and Peru have cut mortality by roughly half but still face higher maternal and adolescent fertility rates. Service coverage (skilled births, antenatal care, contraception) has expanded, and Peru has dramatically reduced child stunting.

Below I give **story‑ready trend bullets** you can drop straight into your article.

---

## 1. Under‑5 mortality (per 1,000 live births), 2000–2023

**Chile**

- Fell from about <claim id="4a2bd64e" policy="auto">10.9</claim> deaths per 1,000 in 2000 to <claim id="8ed10239" policy="auto">7.2</claim> in 2023.  
- Most of the decline happened before 2010; since then the curve has flattened, reflecting that Chile is already at very low levels.

**Colombia**

- Dropped from about <claim id="1bffe658" policy="auto">25.1</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="f78e1b01" policy="auto">12.0</claim> in 2023—roughly a halving over two decades.  
- The decline was steady: mid‑2000s values around the low‑20s, mid‑2010s around the mid‑teens, and just above 10 today.

**Peru**

- Fell from about <claim id="b2a36739" policy="auto">37.9</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="30596b53" policy="auto">15.8</claim> in 2023—more than a 50% reduction.  
- Big gains in the 2000s (from the high‑30s to low‑20s by 2010), then a slower but continued decline in the 2010s.

**Interpretation for your article:**  
All three countries have **more than halved the risk of dying before age 5** since 2000, with Peru showing the steepest relative improvement, closing much of the gap with Chile.

---

## 2. Neonatal mortality (first 28 days, per 1,000 live births), 2000–2023

**Chile**

- From about <claim id="c7310a48" policy="auto">5.8</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="5f1a8627" policy="auto">4.6</claim> in 2023.  
- Very modest decline because levels were already low.

**Colombia**

- From about <claim id="4e2ff15f" policy="auto">13.5</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="2c89c155" policy="auto">6.5</claim> in 2023—roughly halved.  

**Peru**

- From about <claim id="169f9e89" policy="auto">15.8</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="c426d4ba" policy="auto">7.8</claim> in 2023—again about a 50% reduction.

**Interpretation:**  
Neonatal deaths have fallen substantially in Colombia and Peru, but they now account for an even larger share of remaining child deaths, highlighting the importance of quality care around birth.

---

## 3. Maternal mortality ratio (per 100,000 live births), 2000–2023

**Chile**

- Around <claim id="f4e964d9" policy="auto">33</claim> maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000, down to <claim id="a693f2f4" policy="auto">10</claim> in 2023.  
- Chile crossed into “very low” territory by the early 2010s (values in the mid‑teens) and has remained there.

**Colombia**

- Around <claim id="e8343654" policy="auto">95</claim> in 2000, peaking slightly in the mid‑2000s, then falling to the 60–70 range by the late 2010s.  
- A COVID‑era spike is visible: <claim id="97327084" policy="auto">147</claim> in 2021, then back down to <claim id="9e397587" policy="auto">59</claim> by 2023.

**Peru**

- From about <claim id="d8b576bb" policy="auto">115</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="2e75d199" policy="auto">51</claim> in 2023.  
- Progress was strong in the 2000s (down to double digits by around 2010), but like Colombia, Peru saw a sharp temporary rise during 2020–2021 (<claim id="966312f6" policy="auto">141</claim> in 2021) before dropping again.

**Interpretation:**  
All three have **cut maternal deaths by roughly half or more** since 2000. Chile now has levels similar to high‑income countries; Colombia and Peru have improved but remain several times higher, and the pandemic temporarily reversed some gains.

---

## 4. Skilled birth attendance (% of births), 2000–2021

**Chile**

- Already near‑universal in 2000: about <claim id="d70725be" policy="auto">99.8</claim>%.  
- Remained at or above <claim id="efcc718e" policy="auto">99.8</claim>% through 2019.

**Colombia**

- Rose from around <claim id="2f6e07b0" policy="auto">86.1</claim>% in 2000 to about <claim id="de9bd242" policy="auto">98.8</claim>% in 2019.  
- Big jump in the early 2000s, then consolidation above 95%.

**Peru**

- From roughly <claim id="560114b5" policy="auto">59.3</claim>% in 2000 to <claim id="c1ffa4be" policy="auto">94.9</claim>% in 2021.  
- Particularly rapid increases between 2000 and 2010 (from the high‑50s to the low‑80s), then further gains to the mid‑90s.

**Interpretation:**  
By the 2010s, **almost all births in all three countries were attended by skilled staff**, with Peru showing the most dramatic expansion from a low baseline.

---

## 5. Antenatal care (at least one visit, % of pregnant women)

**Peru**

- Improved from about <claim id="8d6b8e68" policy="auto">83.8</claim>% in 2000 to around <claim id="b8cb8c36" policy="auto">98.1</claim>% in 2020.  
- The increase was steady, crossing 90% in the mid‑2000s and approaching universal coverage by the late 2010s.

**Colombia**

- Data show high coverage throughout: from about <claim id="6e14357b" policy="auto">90.8</claim>% in 2000 to around <claim id="d4e89b6e" policy="auto">97.2</claim>% by 2016.

**Interpretation:**  
Both Peru and Colombia now provide **antenatal care to nearly all pregnant women**, suggesting that remaining maternal deaths are more about quality and timeliness of care than initial contact.

---

## 6. Child nutrition – stunting and wasting (Peru, Colombia, Chile)

### Stunting (% of children under 5 who are too short for their age)

**Peru**

- From about <claim id="7d5c173a" policy="auto">31.3</claim>% in 2000 to <claim id="8464ea8a" policy="auto">11.5</claim>% in 2023.  
- That’s a reduction of roughly two‑thirds in just over two decades—one of Latin America’s standout success stories.

**Colombia**

- From about <claim id="de44995c" policy="auto">18.2</claim>% in 2000 to <claim id="b68b58c4" policy="auto">12.7</claim>% in 2016 (latest in this series).  
- A modest but clear decline, with stunting now around the low‑teens.

**Chile**

- Already very low: around <claim id="a9fcb155" policy="auto">2.8</claim>% in 2001, and about <claim id="3498fd40" policy="auto">1.8</claim>% by 2014 (latest).  
- Stunting is now rare at the national level, though pockets may remain.

### Wasting (% of children under 5 who are too thin for their height)

**Peru**

- Around <claim id="76f46e47" policy="auto">1.1</claim>% in 2000, fluctuating around 0.4–1.0% in the 2010s, and at <claim id="5a7bb741" policy="auto">0.6</claim>% in 2023.  
- Wasting has been low and stable; the main problem was chronic undernutrition (stunting), which has improved sharply.

**Colombia**

- Around <claim id="05854d07" policy="auto">1.0</claim>% in 2000, down to about <claim id="9c578ad8" policy="auto">1.6</claim>% in 2016—values remain low but somewhat variable.

**Chile**

- Around <claim id="644078e5" policy="auto">0.5</claim>% in 2001 and similarly low (around <claim id="0f41d577" policy="auto">0.3</claim>–<claim id="77f6d4fd" policy="auto">0.5</claim>%) in later years.

**Interpretation:**  
The big story is **Peru’s dramatic fall in stunting**, bringing it closer to Colombia’s levels, while Chile has maintained stunting near zero and wasting very low.

---

## 7. Adolescent fertility (births per 1,000 women aged 15–19), 2000–2023

**Chile**

- From about <claim id="e8627c5d" policy="auto">61.242</claim> in 2000 to just <claim id="95148b00" policy="auto">6.542</claim> in 2023.  
- That’s an almost 90% decline, moving Chile from high to very low adolescent fertility within one generation.

**Colombia**

- From about <claim id="97d6797c" policy="auto">94.496</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="26232d7e" policy="auto">59.473</claim> in 2023.  
- The rate has fallen but remains high by regional and global standards; progress has been slower than in Chile.

**Peru**

- From about <claim id="415b706e" policy="auto">73.504</claim> in 2000 to <claim id="fa7d452e" policy="auto">43.562</claim> in 2023.  
- A significant decline, yet still nearly seven times Chile’s rate.

**Interpretation:**  
Adolescent fertility has dropped everywhere, but **Chile has virtually eliminated teen childbearing**, while Colombia and Peru still face high rates that drive maternal and child health risks and social inequality.

---

## 8. Contraceptive prevalence, modern methods (% of married women 15–49)

**Peru**

- From about <claim id="7f5ac533" policy="auto">50.4</claim>% in 2000 to <claim id="b33d8cb8" policy="auto">57.9</claim>% in 2023.  
- Gradual increase, with a plateau around the mid‑50s in the 2010s.

**Colombia**

- From about <claim id="dcae1614" policy="auto">64</claim>% in 2000 to around <claim id="0dc3d3ca" policy="auto">75.9</claim>% by 2015 (latest).  
- High and rising use of modern contraception, consistent with falling fertility and later childbearing.

**Chile**

- Around <claim id="0ec42d60" policy="auto">64.2</claim>% in 2006 and about <claim id="7654c463" policy="auto">69.84</claim>% in 2016 (latest).  
- Modern method use is high and appears to have increased moderately.

**Interpretation:**  
Higher contraceptive use in **Chile and Colombia** aligns with lower fertility and, in Chile’s case, very low adolescent fertility. Peru has improved but still lags, which helps explain its higher teen pregnancy.

---

## How to frame this evolution in your article

You might summarize the long‑term story as:

- **“From survival to quality”** – Child and maternal deaths have been halved or more since 2000 in all three countries, shifting the agenda from basic access to the quality of care, especially around birth and for high‑risk groups.  
- **“Peru’s catch‑up”** – Peru started the 2000s with much worse child health and nutrition but has made some of the **fastest gains in under‑5 mortality and stunting**, now approaching Colombia and, in some indicators, narrowing the gap with Chile.  
- **“The unfinished agenda: adolescent fertility and maternal risk”** – Despite progress, **Colombia and Peru still have high adolescent fertility and higher maternal mortality**, pointing to persistent gaps in sexual and reproductive health services, gender norms, and social protection.

---

## Sources

- **World Bank — World Development Indicators (WB_WDI)**  
  - Mortality rate, under‑5 (per 1,000 live births)  
  - Mortality rate, neonatal (per 1,000 live births)  
  - Maternal mortality ratio (modeled estimate, per 100,000 live births)  
  - Births attended by skilled health staff (% of total)  
  - Pregnant women receiving prenatal care (%)  
  - Prevalence of stunting and wasting (% of children under 5)  
  - Adolescent fertility rate (births per 1,000 women ages 15–19)  
  - Contraceptive prevalence, any modern method (% of married women ages 15–49)

---

**Suggested follow-ups:**

1. Could you create 1–2 simple comparison charts (e.g., under‑5 mortality and adolescent fertility over time) for these three countries?  
2. Can you help me draft three short country narratives (one for each country) that weave these trends into a compelling story?  
3. Can we look at how these health trends relate to changes in income, poverty, or health spending over the same period?
